newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria triumphs in battle for Creditanstalt.
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria triumphs in battle for Creditanstalt.

text.p: Bank Austria said on Sunday its hard-fought victory in the battle for rival Creditanstalt would turn Austria's cozy financial sector on its head and let shareholders and taxpayers laugh all the way to the bank.

Closing the book on Europe's longest privatisation after 11 hours of crisis talks, leaders of Austria's feuding government coalition agreed on Bank Austria as the new owner of the state's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt.
The sale of Creditanstalt, former banker to the Habsburg family of Austro-Hungarian emperors, had split the coalition of dominant Social Democrats and conservative People's Party.

A last-minute deal saved the government from collapse, but at a hefty price for the conservatives who lost their key fight to keep conservative stronghold Creditanstalt out of reach of Social-Democratic controlled Bank Austria.
Social Democrat Finance Minister Viktor Klima hailed the agreement as a breakthrough for Austria's taxpayers.
"The sale was successful, especially for the interests of the Austrian taxpayer and for shareholders of Creditanstalt. We managed to get the best possible price," he said.

Executives of Creditanstalt, faced with the likelihood of having to clear out their desks soon, declined to comment. A defeated and disillusioned group of suitors led by insurer EA-Generali merely said they regretted the decision.

Meanwhile, Bank Austria revelled in the glow of having become the country's most powerful financial and industrial force by a long stretch in return for 17.2 billion schillings ($1.55 billion) in cash, to be paid into the state's bank account by Thursday.

"Based on conservative estimates the future results of the Bank Austria-CA group should bring in extra earnings potential of several billion schillings," chief executive Gerhard Randa, 52, told a hastily convened news conference.
Brandishing a copy of the contract, the dapper career banker added earnings per share of the new Austrian banking behemoth were projected to double in the space of five years.
Analysts took a decidedly more cautious stance, saying the sale may have put an end to political infighting but warning that the potential for synergies would be difficult to realise.

"The general inefficiency within the Austrian banking system makes me very dubious about whether they can actually get the synergy gains they need," said Victoria Maxwell, Austria analyst at James Capel in London.

"(The sale) solved the problem of getting the government some money but it's opened up a whole new can of worms in terms of what they can make of it and I'm sceptical they can make very much," she added.

Randa, all smiles and handshakes after suddenly getting control of what will be one of Europe's top 30 banks, admitted the merger would result in "substantial" charges against earnings, but told Reuters current-year profits should still be above last year's.
He projected 1996 parent operating profit at 5.1 billion schillings, up five percent from the previous year.
Creditanstalt, established in 1855 to finance the development of the Austrian empire's railway network, will be allowed to retain its independence for the next five years.

But at the same time Bank Austria -- controlled by the City of Vienna and part-owned by the state -- will gradually be taken out of the public sector's realm. The state's 19 percent in the bank will be floated and the City of Vienna's influence reduced to below 20 percent within seven years.

The marriage of Austria's two top banks will create a financial powerhouse with some 1,300 billion schillings in total assets, controlling 70 percent of commercial banking and 80 percent of Vienna bourse trade. ($1=11.09 Schilling)
